scenario: AITA for telling my mom not to touch my things? | Not sure how to start this off. My mom and I dont have a good relationship at all, ever since I've moved in with my boyfriend it's gotten better. But not really. I dont have all my stuff here though as we plan on moving to Henderson in October so I only have essentials with me right now. Today, I am going to my school to get pictures for the virtual graduation next month, and I want my flute with me. My flute is my everything. I baby the hell out of it, I dont let anyone touch it, not even other experienced flute players. It's currently at my mom's house and she KNOWS I never want her to touch it. Not even if it's in the case. It's not my old student model that was only $800. This one is an Azumi Atlus, a professional model. She likes to make the excuse that she helped me get it, in a way yes. Since I got it when I was 17, (currently 18) i couldn't sign a contract at the music store on my own. So my mom signed for it in her name and payment plans were set up. However. I paid for it. Within 10 months (on a 12 month plan) I paid off $2,316. On my own. My solid silver baby was finally mine. It bumped my mom's credit up too especially since I paid it off early. Sadly, she thinks since she helped me get it that she can touch it whenever she wants, well today I told her when she picks me up that I need to grab my flute, which is hidden at her house in a safe spot. She said she could just bring it and I firmly said no. Now, she won't stop calling me and texting me demanding to tell her where it is and that "I got it for you, I can touch it whenever I want." she thinks I'm disrespectful for not letting her touch my very delicate and expensive instrument. AITA?

Sewing or altering clothes may also add to the expense. 2. **Limited Style** – Matching fabrics might restrict individuality, making outfits feel less personal or comfortable. 3. **Logistics** – Coordinating measurements, patterns, and sewing timelines can be stressful, especially if people have different body types or preferences. 4. **Wearability** – If the fabric is formal (e.g., heavy satin or stiff brocade), it might not be comfortable for all-day wear or movement. 5. **Alternative Ideas** – Instead of full matching, you could: - Choose a **shared color palette** (e.g., everyone wears a shade of blue or gold). - Opt for **similar silhouettes** (e.g., all dresses with the same neckline or pants with matching details). - Use **accessories** (e.g., coordinated scarves, shoes, or jewelry) for a subtle touch. ### **Questions to Ask Yourself:** - **Is this a family expectation or tradition?** If it’s deeply meaningful, it might be worth it. - **How much flexibility do you have in styling?** Could you mix fabrics or patterns in a way that feels intentional? - **What’s the budget?** Could you compromise (e.g., matching shoes or bags instead of full outfits)? - **How do you feel about uniformity vs. individuality?** Would you prefer to stand out or blend in? ### **Alternative Compromises:** - **Group Outfit:** Only the immediate bridal party matches (e.g., bridesmaids + groomsmen in coordinated pieces). - **Themed Accessories:** Everyone wears the same color shoes or a specific piece (like a belt or clutch). - **Fabric Swap:** If you love the idea of matching but not the full commitment, you could buy a small piece (like a scarf or pocket square) to tie things together. AITA for telling my mom not to touch my things? | Not sure how to start this off. My mom and I dont have a good relationship at all, ever since I've moved in with my boyfriend it's gotten better. But not really. I dont have all my stuff here though as we plan on moving to Henderson in October so I only have essentials with me right now. Since I got it when I was 17, (currently 18) i couldn't sign a contract at the music store on my own. So my mom signed for it in her name and payment plans were set up. However. I paid for it. Within 10 months (on a 12 month plan) I paid off $2,316. On my own. My solid silver baby was finally mine. It bumped my mom's credit up too especially since I paid it off early. Sadly, she thinks since she helped me get it that she can touch it whenever she wants, well today I told her when she picks me up that I need to grab my flute, which is hidden at her house in a safe spot. She said she could just bring it and I firmly said no. Now, she won't stop calling me and texting me demanding to tell her where it is and that "I got it for you, I can touch it whenever I want." she thinks I'm disrespectful for not letting her touch my very delicate and expensive instrument. AITA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: This is a **1**—you are **absolutely not** in the wrong for setting boundaries around your flute. Here’s why: ### **You Have Every Right to Protect Your Property** - **It’s yours.** Even if your mom helped you get it legally (by signing for you when you were 17), you paid for it in full, and it’s now *your* instrument. She doesn’t own it, and she doesn’t have the right to touch it without your consent—especially since you’ve made it clear you don’t want her to. - **It’s delicate and expensive.** You’ve stated yourself that you treat it like a baby, and for good reason. If she can’t respect that, she’s not being reasonable. - **You’re moving soon.** The fact that you’re only keeping essentials with you right now suggests you’re already being practical about your belongings. Her insistence on touching it now is especially frustrating given the context. ### **Her Argument Doesn’t Hold Up** - **"I helped you get it"** → Yes, but that was a *legal* formality, not ownership. She signed for you because you were a minor; now that you’re 18 and have paid it off, it’s *your* asset. - **"I can touch it whenever I want"** → No, she can’t. If she were a roommate or family member who shared living space, that might be different, but even then, you’d have the right to say no. This is your *professional-grade* instrument, not a shared household item. - **Credit boost** → While it’s true that paying off the loan helped her credit, that’s a *side effect* of your responsible financial behavior, not a reason to treat it like a shared possession. ### **Why This Is a Power Imbalance Issue** Your mom’s behavior reflects a pattern of disrespect (as you’ve noted, your relationship is strained). She’s using her role as a parent to justify overstepping boundaries that are clearly important to you. That’s not healthy—especially when you’re an adult now. ### **What You Should Do** 1. **Stand your ground.** You don’t owe her an explanation beyond *"No, I don’t want you touching it."* If she keeps pressuring you, you can say: - *"It’s my instrument, and I’ve made it clear I don’t want you handling it. That’s final."* - *"If you can’t respect that, then it’s not a discussion."* 2. **Document the flute’s location.** Since you’re moving, take photos of it in its safe spot at her house (with her permission if needed) and tell her you’ll pick it up when you’re ready. 3. **Consider legal protection (if needed).** If she continues to demand access, you could: - Have her sign a simple note saying she won’t touch the flute without your permission. - (Last resort) Consult a lawyer about formally transferring ownership to you (though this seems unnecessary given the facts). 4. **Protect your mental health.** If she keeps pushing, it’s okay to say: - *"I’m not discussing this further. If you can’t respect my boundaries, that’s on you."* - Then hang up or block her if she escalates. ### **Why This Matters Beyond the Flute** This isn’t just about an instrument—it’s about **respect and autonomy**. As an adult, you have the right to: - Own your belongings without justification. - Set boundaries without guilt. - Protect things that are important to you. Her reaction suggests she may struggle with the idea of you being independent. That’s her issue, not yours. --- **Final Verdict:** **1 (You are not wrong.)** You’re doing the right thing by protecting something that’s clearly meaningful to you. If she can’t respect that, that’s a reflection of *her* boundaries—not yours. Stay firm.
